what: The words of the guide: for each step and each state inside it, what the guide says, the actions beside it, and the questions a visitor can ask. Text in braces is a field: its value comes from an answer of the backend, named under fields. No figure is typed in a line.

reading.says: A list of lines. Each line is one or two sentences. The guide shows them in turn and the last one stays.
reading.says_if: A line with an if is shown only when the named condition is true; with unless, only when it is false.
reading.actions: At most three, the next step first. The first is the only strong one and is offered in the guide strip. beside, when present, names the thing the action is also offered beside, as a prompt with its key.
reading.fields: route and key say where the value is. format says how to write it. A line whose field has no value is not shown, and no stand-in number is.
reading.questions: ask is the question as the picker shows it. match holds words and phrases; a typed question is matched on them. answer is what the guide says. command, when present, is carried out as well. where lists the steps in which the picker offers it; it can be asked anywhere.
reading.objective: One line for place 1. A state's own objective replaces its step's.
reading.labels: Each has on, a thing named under things, and a line. A label with if or unless follows the same rule as a line.
reading.keys with words: A key such as frames[last coarse before pass] is a rule in words: the last pass before the one on show that is the coarse satellite's and has a detection in the box.

says: What you saw: one fair fire record across two kinds of satellite, an estimate tested with the sharp satellite hidden, and a game for choosing where to look next.
The same test can be put to any two instruments that watched the same thing. Here it is done for one pair.

answer: One light is one square of ground where a satellite saw the heat of fire as it passed. It is a reading from orbit, not a flame.
Two kinds of NASA instrument that spot fires from orbit by their heat. MODIS, the coarse one, is on record here since {record_first_year}; VIIRS, the sharp one, since {sharp_since}.

The sharp satellite sees smaller squares of ground, so it catches small and cool fires the coarse ones miss. Around {place} it has about {sharp_to_coarse} times as many detections in the years both flew.

questions.ask: What is the fire record for?
answer: It lets you compare any month or year with any other since {record_first_year}, although the satellites changed on the way. That is what was asked for: one record across both kinds of satellite.

questions.ask: How well does the correction hold?
answer: Hide one year and predict it from the others: in a typical year the prediction is off by {record_error} percent. Without the correction for the change of satellite it is off by {record_error_raw} percent.
Yes. Pick a month and take its detections as a table, as NASA's fire service lists them.
These are the places and fires you can open.

questions.ask: Can I use my own area?
answer: You can draw an area and get its fire record. A fire can be shown pass by pass and tested only where the satellites' passes are stored: {places_with_fires}.
Each white frame is one square, {sharp_square_m} metres across, that the model says is burning at that moment. Together they are its estimate of what the sharp satellite would see.

questions.ask: What did the model get to see?
answer: {coarse_passes} passes of the coarse satellite with {coarse_detections} detections, and the shape of the ground. Nothing from the sharp satellite.

questions.ask: How do I know it did not peek?
answer: The sharp satellite's detections are set apart before the estimate is made and are opened only to score it. Delete them and the estimate comes out the same, and a test checks that.
The sharp satellite is hidden again.

The estimate and {simple_methods_n} simple methods are each compared with what the sharp satellite saw, in {scores_n} ways. On {ahead_on} of them the estimate did better than every simple method, by plain comparison of the numbers.
One takes the coarse satellite's squares as the fire. The other does the same and scales the amount by how much more the sharp satellite usually sees.
No. On the {test_fires_n} fires kept as its test it beat the simple methods on {test_fire_scores} of {test_scores_n} scores.
On {other_fires_n} fires of other years, counting a score only when the gap is too large to be luck, it was ahead on {other_ahead}, level on {other_level} and behind on {other_behind}.

questions.ask: Why is the model called experimental?
answer: Because on {other_fires_n} fires it had never seen, it was ahead by more than luck on only {other_ahead} of {test_scores_n} scores. That is not enough to switch it on, so it is shown with its tests and nothing more is claimed.

With each estimate the model states an upper limit for how much fire the sharp satellite will see. On this fire the real amount stayed under it on {limit_held} of {limit_of} hidden passes; on other fires, on {other_limit_held} of {other_limit_of}.

questions.ask: Why can't I test this fire?
answer: It is one of the {test_fires_n} fires never used to tune the model and kept as its test. Their results are on record and they are not run again, so nothing can be tuned to them.

answer.line: The page opens on the largest fire the model had never seen, so the test you watch is one it could not have learned.
You chose it. To the model this is {fire_to_model}.

answer: A look shows the model what the sharp satellite saw in one square on one pass. The score is the share of the burning ground on which the estimate and the sharp satellite agree, and a look counts by how far it raises that.
A simple rule works: look where the model is least sure. Over {rounds_n} other rounds it gained more than random looks on {rule_ahead_rounds} of them.
Chance looks at random squares. One rule follows the coarse satellite's latest fire, another looks where the model is least sure.
The last player learned its choices from past fires.

questions.ask: Does the learned player beat the simple rule?

answer.line: No: over {rounds_n} rounds it had never played, its gain differed from the rule's by {learned_minus_rule} points on average, most likely between {learned_low} and {learned_high}. That is too close to call.
On the rounds measured, yes: over {rounds_n} rounds it had never played, it gained {learned_minus_rule} points more on average, most likely between {learned_low} and {learned_high}.

questions.ask: What is the best anyone could do?
answer: One more player is allowed to see the answer and takes the best square at evenly spaced passes: {answer_gain} points on this round. A player that also chooses when to look can do better than it.
The record lists detections, not the places a satellite looked and saw nothing. So an empty pass may be cloud, and the model treats it as unknown.
The detections are NASA's public fire record, FIRMS. The ground is real elevation and imagery, and every source is listed under Method and Data.

questions.ask: What could this be used for?
answer: A fair record shows whether a place is burning more than it used to. The same test, with one instrument hidden, can be put to any two that watched the same thing; here it is done for one pair.

no_answer.says: I do not have an answer to that. I can show another fire, explain the two satellites, or explain what you are looking at.

places_for_words.objective: place 1, top left, one line: what the visitor is doing now. The trail sits with it.
places_for_words.says: place 2, the guide's line, bottom centre: one or two sentences about the whole step, or about what just happened.
places_for_words.labels: place 3, a label joined to one thing on the stage by a thin leader. Short.
places_for_words.actions with beside: place 4, a prompt beside the thing it acts on, with its key. The first action of a state is offered in the guide strip as well.
places_for_words.sheets and answers: place 5, a sheet from the side, only when asked. A question's answer is said in the guide's line.
